webTitle: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom

fields.headline: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom
fields.trailText: Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the US supreme court on Sunday to allow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judge had blocked new limits on such ballots, just ahead of November’s midterm elections. The latest filing follows a decision by US district court judge Indira Talwani on Friday to extend a court order preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Donald Trump’s executive order. The legal fight was continuing as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail – giving the administration little time to make major changes to the rules. “Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more states will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place – including Alabama on September 9 and at least five states the week of September 13,” the solicitor general, John Sauer, said in the filing to the supreme court on Sunday. “Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them. And while the injunction allows the Postal Service and the states to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements … each day the injunction is in place risks sowing confusion and chaos because the injunction makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer continued in the emergency application. It is the third time the administration has asked the highest court in the US to step into the dispute and that court has allowed the plan to move forward but has not decided whether it was legal. The outcome of the wrangling could have significant consequences for this year’s elections, with control of Congress on the line. Nearly one-third of US voters cast their ballots by mail. The US president signed an executive order in March that would prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots – ie only to voters on approved lists. Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the ordered changes are unconstitutional, while state election officials who run the elections say there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives. The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” which are aimed at protecting voting security, and further called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”. Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite having often used the method himself. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud. The USPS has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted. The Associated Press contributed reporting

webTitle: This smokejumper says the US has lost its empathy. That’s why he’s running for Congress

fields.headline: This smokejumper says the US has lost its empathy. That’s why he’s running for Congress
fields.trailText: Montana’s Sam Forstag says US working class is left playing a game of chance while neither party serves its interests
fields.bodyText: At around five o’clock on a winter evening in 2013, then college student Sam Forstag was driving through a snowstorm toward his third job of the day, making sandwiches at the Subway inside a Walmart. “I was always late,” Forstag recalled with a laugh more than a decade later. Halfway there, the gray sedan in front of him lost traction. It spun across the icy road and slid nose-first into a ditch. Forstag’s first instinct was to pull over. Growing up in a tight-knit community in North Portland, Oregon, and later in Montana, he had learned that when someone’s car ended up in a ditch, you stopped. You grabbed a shovel or you called a neighbor. You helped push the car back on to the road. That was simply what people did. But he kept driving. “I remember thinking, ‘I should stop – but I don’t have time,’” he said. He couldn’t afford to lose the job that helped pay his rent, car payment and groceries. He thought about it for the rest of that sandwich-making shift. That memory has become part of Forstag’s political identity as a firefighter turned Democratic candidate hoping to flip Montana’s first congressional district in November’s midterm election. Once a scholarship kid at a Catholic high school, 32-year-old Forstag has built his campaign around a deeply personal argument: that the economic pressures consuming many Americans do more than empty their wallets. They leave people with less time and capacity to care for one another. That message has helped Forstag galvanize young and working-class voters in a district that has long favored Republicans. “There are a lot of people in this country who don’t have the time,” he said. “It’s much harder to extend the kind of compassion your neighbors deserve when you’re working three jobs just to get by.” He sees Donald Trump-era politics as a consequence of years of economic struggle that has shattered the lives of working-class people. And he believes that politicians such as the president exploit that desperation, he said, turning economic anxiety into anti-immigrant rhetoric and culture-war battles while voters’ material conditions continue to deteriorate. “If your life is getting materially worse year after year, and you vote for the party out of power, that’s how democracy works. People who vote [for the opposition] are rightfully disillusioned and frustrated with the entire system because the system has not served them for too damn long,” he said. But his own life story gives him reason to think there’s another way out. Forstag grew up in a single-parent household in which his mother, an intensive care nurse, worked overnight shifts to raise her children. “I remember being a nine-year-old who was worried that Mom was working too much,” he said. On days when she had to work overnight, she would drop him and his sister at a friend’s house at about 6am. By the time school ended, she was often still at the hospital. Friends’ parents would drive him home, or he’d frequently ride his bike home: a $20 pink garage sale find, complete with sparkly decorations that were supposed to embarrass him when he’d lost a previous bike (“instead, I loved it,” he said). But what he remembers most is not how hard his mother worked, but how after a full emergency room shift, his mother didn’t treat caring for others as extraordinary. The fire inside By the time he turned 30, Forstag felt he had finally found stability, a place to call home and, most important, his community. And it came through smokejumping, or parachuting into fire zones to put out the blaze. Smokejumping was the first career that gave Forstag health insurance, a retirement account, and a paycheck steady enough to cover his mortgage and student loans. For eight fire seasons, he and his crew dropped into remote terrain to battle some of the country’s most dangerous fires. The work was physically brutal and often dangerous, but the people who stood beside him became more than co-workers. Many came from backgrounds that felt familiar to him – working-class families, small town residents, people who depended on the job not only for a paycheck but for healthcare, retirement and a sense of purpose. Then, after Trump returned to the White House in 2025, that sense of security began to unravel. Trump had campaigned on reducing government and appointed Elon Musk to lead the “department of government efficiency” (Doge), which oversaw sweeping reductions in the federal workforce. Among those affected were smokejumpers and other federal wildland firefighters in Montana. Friends and union colleagues who had spent years risking their lives fighting wildfires suddenly found themselves without jobs or health insurance. “That pissed me off,” Forstag said, voice trembling. Forstag turned to the elected officials he believed were supposed to represent them but found little help from the people who publicly celebrated his industry’s service in the past. “I was pissed off at [retiring incumbent] Ryan Zinke when he was holding his seat,” Forstag said. “When we were going through those cuts, we reached out to him time after time. And I got crickets. That’s a failure of representation. Meanwhile, that guy got $20m richer while sitting in office.” While the Guardian could not independently verify Forstag’s specific claim about $20m, Zinke’s financial disclosures showed significant wealth accumulation while holding public office. Additionally, Zinke faced 18 federal investigations during his tenure as interior secretary, from March 2017 to January 2019, including into real estate dealings in his home town. The Guardian reached out to Zinke’s office multiple times for comment but did not receive a response. For Forstag, the answer was not to abandon politics but to make government work for people like the ones he grew up with. Running for Congress, however, meant risking the first stable life he had ever built. “I have to leave the only retirement I’ve got, that I’ve been building,” he said. “And leaving behind the only healthcare I have. I have to leave the only career I’ve got to risk it all on this.” He spent weeks talking through the decision with friends from the National Federation of Federal Employees (NIFF), a union he led as vice-president. Eventually, he drove alone to one of his favorite lakes in Montana’s Swan Valley, a place so secluded that he refused to tell the Guardian its name. He camped there for the night, beyond cell service, trying to decide whether to abandon the first secure career he had ever known. “I woke up in the morning and decided to do it,” he said. Campaigning from the couch The campaign that followed hardly looked like a congressional operation, though Forstag was almost immediately endorsed by the progressive senator Bernie Sanders. Its headquarters was Forstag’s modest 900-sq-ft house in Missoula, a place he had only recently been able to afford. Staff members crowded on to a shared couch in the living room, making phone calls and texting voters. Volunteers pitched pop-up tents outside and turned the front yard into a makeshift office. Aaron Derry, a 53-year-old physician assistant and lifelong Democratic voter and volunteer, was struck by the energy. “I’ve never seen so many young people show up,” Derry said. “I’ve never seen so many 20-year-olds.” “My 22-year-old daughter, who’s away at college, called me and asked if I was on Sam’s team.” Across western Montana, Forstag’s campaign drew an unusually young coalition of volunteers and first-time supporters. But the frustration of young Montanans did not necessarily translate into enthusiasm for Democrats or even awareness of Forstag. Lukas Kosel, 22, a recent Montana State University graduate, was preparing to leave the state for Baltimore, where he planned to pursue graduate studies in African American studies. Like Forstag, Kosel was raised by a single mother and loves Montana’s open spaces. But almost two months before the election, he hadn’t heard much about the candidate. “I have to do research on him,” he said. “But I imagine he is like any other Democratic candidate” – and that’s not a good thing. “Much of my life, I have seen Democrats or Republicans doing the same things,” he said. “They have all the money to fund the war in the Middle East, but what about our student debt, our future prospects?” That skepticism is precisely what Forstag argues his party has failed to reckon with. “We have a national Democratic party that is refusing to open the doors of change to a lot of young people,” Forstag said. He believes Democrats must make room for a new generation of candidates willing to challenge both the party establishment and long-held political assumptions. In some ways, Forstag fits neatly within that surging movement. He rejected support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), called for conditioning US assistance to Israel on what he described as “strictly enforced humanitarian requirements” and connected increases in military spending to quality of life at home. “We’re in another war, in Iran, that nobody wants, talking about hundreds of billions of dollars,” he said. “That is not helping anybody’s life here in the States.” Two-party criticism In May, the congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders came to Montana to campaign for Forstag, in an event that galvanized young voters across the state. Four months after entering the race, Forstag defeated the Democratic establishment’s preferred candidate by nearly five percentage points, pulling off one of the biggest primary upsets in recent Montana politics. Montana’s first congressional district stretches across the western half of the state, encompassing liberal college towns, fast-growing mountain communities and vast rural counties that have long favored Republicans. While Trump remains deeply popular across much of the district and endorsed conservative radio host Aaron Flint to succeed Zinke, Democratic strongholds such as Missoula and Bozeman have made the seat a genuinely competitive congressional district in Montana. Again and again, Forstag returns to the same argument: Democrats have spent too much time debating ideology and too little time listening to the economic frustrations shaping everyday life in places like Montana. “And I find that so damn frustrating,” he said. “Six months ago, everybody said affordability is the thing to talk about. Well, where the hell have y’all been living for the last 10 years? Here in Montana, every time I go to a bar, that’s what people are talking about. ‘My rent went up $100.’ ‘Mine went up $150.’ This isn’t new. Somebody just came up with a buzzword for it.” A poll conducted in late April and early May showed that 62% of Montana voters reported difficulty affording healthcare, and 61% struggled with gas and transportation costs. Those anxieties are not unique to Montana. A March Gallup poll found that 51% of Americans worried about the economy “a great deal”. Another poll found that 77% of Americans rated the economy poorly. “One party was saying the economy’s better than you think it is,” he continued. “The other was saying the system’s broken. Unfortunately, the latter was lying about everything they were going to do to fix it.” Though focused on his Republican opponents, Forstag is critical of how the left operates too. He believes progressives became too focused on cultural battles at the expense of material concerns. He wanted the energy of the left without what he saw as its blind spots. Some voters share the concern. Mary Brower, 62, a retired high school teacher in Bozeman and a lifelong Democrat, believes Forstag has struck a chord with younger voters. But she worries about the limits of progressive politics in Montana. “I just worry that Sam will be seen as too liberal,” Brower said. “Most Montana voters are still more centrist. Even though he’s in favor of a lot of liberal causes, I think he’s got to walk the center line as much as possible while still being honest and authentic.” But earlier this month, Forstag won the endorsement of the Blue Dog Coalition, the moderate and centrist Democratic caucus in the House, an endorsement that unsettled some of his progressive supporters. And the Montana Democratic party chair, Shannan O’Brien, said Forstag’s message reflects a broader frustration with politics as usual. “People are ready for a change,” she said. “People are exhausted hearing the same thing in Washington over and over again, and they heard something different from Sam.” O’Brien’s defense of Forstag comes at a moment when the national Democratic party is facing growing tensions between its moderate, establishment wing and a newer generation of younger, more progressive candidates. In recent cycles, many progressive insurgents have ousted moderate incumbents, prompting some establishment Democrats to criticize what they see as a dangerous populist shift. How big is this tent? Forstag’s economic message and his willingness to engage with Republicans have resonated beyond his Democratic constituents. More than five Republican former and current legislators have endorsed him. Brian Putnam, a former Republican legislator from Kalispell who represented one of Montana’s most Republican-leaning districts, is among them. “I was in the Montana legislature for the 2021 session as a Republican, and that’s where I met Sam,” he said. Despite their different parties, Putnam respected Forstag, who was lobbying at the time for the ACLU. “He’s a straight shooter,” Putnam said. “He’s a guy you could come to and ask about something, and whether it’s good for him or not, he’s going to give you the correct answer.” What impressed Putnam most was Forstag’s ability to work across party lines. Endorsing Forstag put Putnam at odds with his own party. But he believes Montana Republicans should reject Trump’s approach to politics. “I disagree with a lot of Trump’s policies,” he said. “I don’t think that Trump actually has policies. He has whims and things.” Still, even after endorsing Forstag, Putnam remained skeptical of parts of his campaign. He worried that endorsements from Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez might pull Forstag too far to the left. Aaron Flint, Forstag’s Republican opponent, has sought to portray him as a radical. “Is it radical that you should be able to work one good job and afford a roof over your head?” Forstag said in response. “I don’t think any of that’s radical. I think those are fundamental to what the American dream actually is.” As the election comes closer, Forstag has less than two months to make his final case to skeptics. To win in November, Forstag will need to rebuild the coalition that had carried Jon Tester in 2024 to victory in the district – a coalition of libertarians, right-leaning Democrats and working-class Republicans. One of those libertarians is Zach Lund, a father of two. A Montana native who works as a chef, Lund, 41, said his biggest concerns are civil liberties, military spending and what he sees as an increasing unwillingness to hold powerful people accountable. “You can’t have the largest sex-trafficking case in the history of the United States and not arrest anybody,” Lund said, referring to the Epstein investigation. “What kind of country is that?” “I feel like a lot of people in the country who leaned libertarian are watching the police state come from the very party they thought was going to promote smaller government and personal freedom,” he said. Lund does not plan to vote in the upcoming election. “A lot of times, lately, promises are made, and then they don’t follow through,” he said. “You kind of feel like, ‘This isn’t what I voted for.’ You kind of get sick of getting burned. It’s hard to have that trust in politicians.” Forstag sees in voters like Lund – those wary of politics and the government, consumed by the rising costs of daily life – a version of the young man he once was, driving home on an icy winter evening after working three jobs, too exhausted and financially strapped to stop for a stranger whose car had slipped into a ditch. That moment has become more than a memory to Forstag. It is the question that has shaped both his politics and his campaign: what happens to a democracy when ordinary people become so consumed by survival that they no longer have the time, hope or the compassion to care for one another? “The American dream was not ever supposed to be something that was a game of chance,” Forstag said. “It was supposed to be something that was open to everybody.” In November, Montana voters will decide whether they believe him.

webTitle: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns

fields.headline: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
fields.trailText: Leon Panetta tells Guardian US is risking ‘forever war’ and says Pentagon ‘turmoil’ sending message of weakness
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict. Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight. “It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added. Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings. US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.” He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries. “And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.” In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership. “The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.” The White House was also contacted for comment. In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure. Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said. Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing. The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender. That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East. The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint. “So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said. Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.” He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open. “So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.” Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And when asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.” Panetta said he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it. He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health onboard. “Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said. “So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

webTitle: Game on: November elections kick into high gear with control of Congress in the balance

fields.headline: Game on: November elections kick into high gear with control of Congress in the balance
fields.trailText: Trump is unpopular and inflation is still high – and Democrats are looking to use that to their advantage
fields.bodyText: When voters went to the polls in the 2022 midterm elections, all the ingredients were there for Joe Biden’s allies to suffer a wipeout. The president was unpopular, inflation was high and historical trends predicted voters would take out their frustrations by ending the Democratic party’s control of Congress. But when the ballots were tallied, the gains Republicans expected to make did not quite materialize. They had won the House of Representatives, but only by a slim margin, while Democrats had expanded their majority in the Senate and built up their strength in state legislatures. Four years later, those very same factors are present once again as Republicans prepare in the 3 November midterms to defend the Senate and House majorities they won two years ago, when voters elected Donald Trump president. Like Biden before him, the president is unpopular and inflation is still high, though not as high as it was under his predecessor. And though he and his allies insist otherwise, there are few reasons to believe Trump can beat the historical trend of voters using midterm elections as an opportunity punish the party holding power in Washington. “The out party, typically speaking, is frustrated or even angry at what has happened during the previous two years, and they’re itching to register their disagreements and discontent, and 2026 is going to be no exception,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington who previously advised Democratic presidents. Campaigning is set to intensify following Monday’s Labor Day holiday, a milestone in election years that marks roughly two months until voters head to the polls. Recent public opinion surveys have shown Democratic candidates for House and Senate seats are either ahead of their opponents or in close contention, and major election forecasters have moved their ratings of key races in the party’s favor. But Republicans appear to have an advantage in one important realm, and that’s cash. Though some Democratic candidates like the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and James Talarico, who is running for a Senate seat in Texas, have posted strong fundraising figures, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has $400m that could be deployed to help his allies, while his erstwhile ally Elon Musk has $50m in another Super Pac, which began spending in favor of some Republican candidates last week. Republican-led states have likely limited to some degree the party’s losses in the House by redrawing congressional maps, with the help of a recent supreme court ruling, despite efforts by Democratic-led states to retaliate. “I’ve been saying this over and over, but Republicans are going to defy history in 63 days and we’re going to hold this House majority,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, recently told reporters. *** A little over a year after the September 11 attacks, George W Bush’s Republican allies were able to expand their majorities in the House and Senate in the 2002 midterms, but most other elections have been unpleasant to terrible for the party in power. Bill Clinton lost both chambers in 1994, and Bush suffered the same fate in 2006. In 2010, Barack Obama famously described the major losses suffered by Democrats in his first midterm election as a “shellacking”. Democrats lost control of the Senate four years later. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House, even as they built up their Senate majority. Biden’s first and only midterm – 2022 – stands out for the deus ex machina that appeared in the form of the supreme court’s decision in Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v Wade and ended the constitutional right to abortion. “It was very clear that women were more energized than usual, and that young people were more energized than usual because of one thing: the Dobbs decision. That’s what really changed the direction of the election,” said Larry Sabato, whose Sabato’s Crystal Ball was among the forecasters that in advance of the vote predicted two dozen Democratic losses that year in the House. The pummeling did not come to pass: the GOP netted nine House seats to give them a tiny majority in the lower chamber, while Democrats expanded their control of the Senate by a single seat, and all their incumbents won re-election. Though Trump was out of office during that election, he endorsed and campaigned with Republican candidates and was frequently in the news for his myriad legal troubles. But without actually being on the ballot, congressional Republicans weren’t able to benefit from his popularity, as they would in the 2024 elections. Democrats, meanwhile, seized on Trump’s continued power in the GOP to rally voters opposed to the then former president, boosting themselves in key races, said Aaron Hitefield, a political science professor at Mississippi State University who studied the 2022 election. “Trump rhetoric benefits Democrats electorally and motivates voters, while not equally motivating Republicans,” he said. “This isn’t necessarily anything new; we always have a surge and decline comparing a president’s party in the presidential election year versus a midterm, but it is particularly more pronounced with Trump.” Now back in the White House, Trump’s profile is as high as ever, and he recently announced plans for an unusual midterm convention later this month in Dallas where he’ll personally pitch voters on keeping Republicans in control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency. It’s a tall order – with a majority no bigger than three seats, many things would have to go right for the GOP to hold the House. Winning the Senate is expected to be tougher for Democrats, because the party must capture at least three seats in states Trump won two years ago, including several that elected him by double digits. *** Control of either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s legislative agenda and give their lawmakers subpoena powers they can use to investigate his administration. Party leaders have centered their pitch to voters on the issue of affordability, arguing that the president’s attack on Iran, imposition of tariffs on trading partners, refusal to extend tax credits for Affordable Care Act health plans and cuts to the social safety net have all driven prices higher. “Life has gotten far too expensive in this country, and Republicans don’t give a damn about it,” the Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, told reporters last week. Recent polls of the generic ballot – an important indicator of sentiment in congressional elections – have shown that Democrats have an edge of between three and eight percentage points. But the trend isn’t unanimous. This week, a Harvard CAPS-Harris Poll taken in August showed Republicans with a slight advantage among likely voters. In Washington, the House reconvened last week after a five-week recess, but Johnson opted to cut its schedule for September short by two weeks, which will give representatives the opportunity to return home to campaign. But though it is typical for electioneering to intensify in the 60-some days before the election, Galston believes voters’ perceptions are “baked in”, with the only lingering question being which party can get more of their supporters out to vote. “A lot of people have already made up their minds,” he said. “Especially for Republicans, the question is not so much whether they’re going to cross party lines and vote for Democrats, although I think some will, but whether they’ll get out of bed on election morning.” There, the Democrats appear to be ahead. An Economist/YouGov survey from the final weeks of August showed Democratic voters with a six percentage point lead in enthusiasm, higher than it was earlier in the summer. “It’s hard to get excited about a presidency that has been defined by a complete failure to get prices under control, coupled with a war that is looking increasingly like a fiasco,” Galston said.
